requirements.title: Natural surveillance
requirements.text: Place features, activities, and people so that legitimate users can easily see what happens around them, increasing the perceived risk to offenders.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Sightlines from occupied spaces
requirements.text: Entrances, parking, and approaches are visible from regularly occupied interior spaces and from adjacent public areas.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Landscaping preserves visibility
requirements.text: Vegetation is selected and maintained so that it does not block views of paths, entrances, and windows.

citation.source: Crowe, T. D. and Fennelly, L. J., Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2013
citation.note: paraphrase; specific height rules vary by jurisdiction

requirements.title: Lighting supports surveillance
requirements.text: Lighting lets users see and recognize people along routes and at entrances at night, without glare or dark gaps.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: No concealment or entrapment spots
requirements.text: Routes avoid hiding places and entrapment areas, or such spots are opened up, lit, or covered by surveillance.

citation.source: Crowe, T. D. and Fennelly, L. J., Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2013
citation.note: paraphrase

requirements.title: Natural access control
requirements.text: Use the layout of entrances, paths, landscaping, and barriers to guide people to legitimate destinations and deny easy access elsewhere.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Defined and limited entrances
requirements.text: Public entry is concentrated at a small number of clearly identified entrances; other doors are visibly not for public use.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Wayfinding channels movement
requirements.text: Paths, signage, and site layout lead users to the intended entrance and away from restricted areas.

citation.source: Crowe, T. D. and Fennelly, L. J., Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2013
citation.note: paraphrase

requirements.title: Physical features restrict access
requirements.text: Fencing, landscaping, and grade changes restrict movement into areas where users have no reason to be.

citation.source: Newman, O., Creating Defensible Space, US Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research, 1996
citation.note: paraphrase

requirements.title: Territorial reinforcement
requirements.text: Make ownership of space clear so that users feel responsible for it and intruders feel noticed.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Public to private transitions are marked
requirements.text: Changes from public to semi-private to private space are marked by visible physical cues such as paving, gates, fencing, or landscaping.

citation.source: Newman, O., Creating Defensible Space, US Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research, 1996
citation.note: paraphrase

requirements.title: Ownership and rules are signaled
requirements.text: Signage and site features communicate who owns the space and what use is permitted.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Maintenance and image
requirements.text: Keep the site in good repair so it signals that it is cared for and monitored, and so that other CPTED features keep working.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Prompt repair and cleanup
requirements.text: Vandalism, graffiti, litter, and broken fixtures are removed or repaired within a defined time.

citation.source: Crowe, T. D. and Fennelly, L. J., Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2013
citation.note: paraphrase; 'broken windows' theory is contested in the literature

requirements.title: Ongoing maintenance of CPTED features
requirements.text: Lighting, landscaping, and signage are maintained on a schedule so that surveillance and access control features keep working.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Activity support
requirements.text: Encourage legitimate activity in public and common spaces so that more people are present to observe.

citation.source: ISO 22341:2021, Security and resilience, Protective security, Guidelines for crime prevention through environmental design
citation.note: paraphrase; ISO 22341 is paywalled and not checked

requirements.title: Common areas support legitimate use
requirements.text: Common areas have features or programs that draw legitimate users during operating hours.

citation.source: Crowe, T. D. and Fennelly, L. J., Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2013
citation.note: paraphrase

requirements.title: Vulnerable activities placed in observed locations
requirements.text: Activities that attract offenders (cash handling, deliveries, isolated parking) are placed where they can be observed.

citation.source: Crowe, T. D. and Fennelly, L. J., Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2013
citation.note: paraphrase

requirements.title: Second-generation CPTED (flagged)
requirements.text: Second-generation concepts that address the social conditions around a site. Flagged: these are community-level concepts and are only partly assessable during a site walkthrough.

citation.source: Saville, G. and Cleveland, G., 2nd Generation CPTED: An Antidote to the Social Y2K Virus of Urban Design, paper presented at the 3rd Annual International CPTED Conference, 1998
citation.note: second-generation concept; paraphrase

requirements.title: Social cohesion
requirements.text: Site users and neighbors have opportunities and structures to work together on safety (for example tenant or neighborhood associations).

citation.source: Saville, G. and Cleveland, G., 2nd Generation CPTED: An Antidote to the Social Y2K Virus of Urban Design, paper presented at the 3rd Annual International CPTED Conference, 1998
citation.note: second-generation concept; paraphrase

requirements.title: Connectivity
requirements.text: The site and its users have working relationships with outside agencies and neighboring organizations.

citation.source: Saville, G. and Cleveland, G., 2nd Generation CPTED: An Antidote to the Social Y2K Virus of Urban Design, paper presented at the 3rd Annual International CPTED Conference, 1998
citation.note: second-generation concept; paraphrase

requirements.title: Community culture
requirements.text: Shared events and spaces give users a common sense of place.

citation.source: Saville, G. and Cleveland, G., 2nd Generation CPTED: An Antidote to the Social Y2K Virus of Urban Design, paper presented at the 3rd Annual International CPTED Conference, 1998
citation.note: second-generation concept; paraphrase

requirements.title: Threshold capacity
requirements.text: Land uses that tend to generate crime are kept below the level the area can absorb.

citation.source: Saville, G. and Cleveland, G., 2nd Generation CPTED: An Antidote to the Social Y2K Virus of Urban Design, paper presented at the 3rd Annual International CPTED Conference, 1998
citation.note: second-generation concept; paraphrase

name: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design
sourceEdition: Sentinel model 1.0 based on ISO 22341:2021 and established CPTED literature
publisher: Sentinel Assess (paraphrased from ISO and CPTED literature)
description: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design: how the layout, sightlines, landscaping, signage, and upkeep of a site discourage crime. Walk the grounds by day and by night.
